questions.q: Per this lesson, why is treating a 'best practice' as universal identified as the deepest mistake underlying most of the others?
options: Because best practices are always technically wrong
Because this mistake only applies to Apex development, never to declarative tools
Because Salesforce does not publish any best-practice guidance at all

Because following generic advice like 'always use Flow' without checking whether this org's actual constraints match the context that made that advice correct elsewhere is how a reasonable-sounding rule becomes the wrong answer for a specific scenario
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly ties back to Lesson 1's opening point -- the fix is checking this org's actual needs against the generic advice's original context, rather than applying the advice universally.

questions.q: What is the 'tell' this lesson gives for catching yourself making the 'fashionable side' mistake?
options: If you can't point to a specific fact about this scenario that the decision depends on, you were probably choosing based on how the answer sounds rather than the scenario's actual justification
If the decision took less than five minutes to make
If the decision involves any custom Apex code
If a manager explicitly approved the decision in writing
questions.explain: The lesson gives this as the concrete self-check: a decision genuinely grounded in scenario facts can point to those facts; one chosen for reputation generally can't.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say presenting a tradeoff decision as costless makes it less trustworthy, not more persuasive?
options: Because executives always reject proposals that mention any cost
Because every real tradeoff has a cost, and omitting it means either the cost hasn't been found yet or it's being hidden -- either way, someone discovers it later, usually at a worse moment
Because costless-sounding proposals take longer to write
Because Salesforce requires every ADR to list a dollar cost
questions.explain: This directly echoes Lessons 8 and 15's warnings -- a hidden or missing cost doesn't disappear, it just surfaces later, typically at a less convenient time than if it had been named upfront.

questions.q: What is the 'context-mismatch misapplication' mistake, as described in this lesson?
options: Refusing to ever reuse a rule learned from a previous project
Writing an ADR that is too long

Reusing a rule from one scenario (like 'always use CDC over Platform Events') in a new scenario without checking whether the specific facts that justified the rule the first time are actually present this time
Choosing batch processing for every integration regardless of freshness needs
questions.explain: The fix the lesson gives isn't to distrust every rule, but to check each time whether the facts that made the original rule correct are actually present in the new scenario.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect all six named mistakes back to Lesson 1's three original questions?
options: It argues the six mistakes are unrelated to Lesson 1's framing entirely
It argues the six mistakes replace the need to ever ask Lesson 1's three questions again
It argues Lesson 1's questions only apply to the security-vs-usability tradeoff, not the others

It argues each mistake is, underneath, a failure to honestly answer one of Lesson 1's three questions -- reaching for a generic answer instead of this org's actual need, ignoring the cost side, or skipping the question about context change
questions.explain: The lesson's closing argument is that the discipline built across the whole course is answering those three original questions honestly every time, and each of the six mistakes represents a specific way of failing to do that.
